title: Could the GCC and Iran collaborate to solve the Strait of Hormuz crisis?
gist: With Hormuz traffic down to a handful of daily crossings versus 100+ prewar and Iran institutionalising control via a toll-collecting Persian Gulf Strait Authority, the author proposes a GCC-led technocratic Gulf maritime cooperative mechanism including Iran and Iraq that trades funding for services in exchange for Iran giving up unilateral control.

insights.claim: The Strait of Hormuz sees only a handful of vessel crossings daily versus more than one hundred before the war, and Trump has said the war with Iran will not end until after the November US midterms.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Implies Hormuz disruption persisting at least through November — sustained oil/LNG risk premium and tanker dislocation.
insights.locator: The stalemate in the Strait of Hormuz

insights.claim: Six months of US military and economic pressure, including an announced 'economic D-Day', has not clearly shown it can force the IRGC to reopen the strait.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Don't assume coercion delivers a quick reopening; a negotiated framework may be needed.
insights.locator: For six months, the United States

insights.claim: In early May Iran set up the Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) to collect steep transit fees, launched punishment strikes on tankers that did not coordinate with it, and claimed more than 300 ships had engaged by June; the US tightened sanctions around the body.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Shippers paying PGSA face US sanctions risk while non-payers face strikes — a squeeze on tanker operators and freight/insurance rates.
insights.locator: In early May, Iran moved to establish

insights.claim: The PGSA reportedly demands a two-million-dollar mandatory 'safe passage' toll per vessel.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Toll adds material per-voyage cost for tankers that do transit.

insights.claim: Oman has been negotiating bilaterally with Iran to reopen the strait, but a deal would effectively divide control between the two, short of the Gulf/US demand that no party control the strait; Trump twice threatened to 'blow them up'.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: An Oman-Iran bilateral deal is not a clean reopening signal; watch for multilateral frameworks instead.
insights.locator: Oman, a US ally whose territorial waters

insights.claim: The GCC should launch a Gulf maritime cooperative mechanism, inviting Iran and Iraq, to handle technocratic tasks (environment, navigational safety, search-and-rescue, fishing, lighthouses and buoys) and block unilateral administration of the strait.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A diplomatic off-ramp that could restore Hormuz flows — a catalyst to watch for crude and shipping normalisation.
insights.locator: A true solution to Iran’s closure

insights.claim: The mechanism could build on ROPME, the 1979 Kuwait-based marine environment body to which the GCC states, Iran and Iraq all belong, with oil slicks off Iran and Oman as a galvanising event and demining as a later task.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Existing institutional scaffolding lowers the barrier to a deal.
insights.locator: Recent oil slicks off the coasts

insights.claim: Because Hormuz is a natural strait under UNCLOS with non-suspendable transit rights, mandatory tolls like those of Suez or Panama could violate international law; the Strait of Malacca model of voluntary contributions offers an alternative.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Legal basis for rejecting Iranian tolls; a Malacca-style funding model is the likely template for any settlement.

insights.claim: The mechanism could levy limited dues for mine clearance or post-war clean-up, similar to Russia's icebreaking fee on the Northern Sea Route, and should be ringfenced from sanctions.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Potential residual shipping costs post-settlement, lower than PGSA tolls.
insights.locator: The Gulf maritime mechanism could also charge

insights.claim: Iran, with the Gulf's longest coastline, could receive a larger share of the mechanism's funding for services, offering Tehran a face-saving alternative to transit fees.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A monetisation path that could make Iran accept reopening — key for the timing of any de-escalation.

insights.claim: Iran's leverage from controlling the strait depreciates daily as Gulf states expand pipelines to the Gulf of Oman or Red Sea and use sea-land routes through Egypt, China cuts seaborne fossil fuel dependence, and US forces improve stealth tanker escorts.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Beneficiaries: bypass pipelines and alternative routes; long-run, Hormuz risk premium should fade as workarounds scale.
insights.quote: Iran has now played its strategic ace in the hole, and IRGC decisionmakers must surely recognize that the value of unilaterally controlling the strait depreciates further with each passing day.

insights.claim: Kuwait and Qatar are especially vulnerable to Iranian control of the strait because they lack alternative export routes that bypass it.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Qatari LNG and Kuwaiti crude supply are most exposed — relevant for LNG prices and those sovereigns' fiscal positions.
insights.locator: At the same time, the Gulf states cannot accept

insights.claim: Iran has sought to monetise its position either via PGSA tolls or a deal with the Trump administration promising sanctions relief, unfrozen assets and investment in return for reopening the strait.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A sanctions-relief-for-reopening deal is a live scenario with large implications for Iranian oil supply.
